A Majorana energy spectrum, associated with fractional quantum Hall states at $\nu = 5/2$, typically manifests as a double peak in tunneling conductance. However, the interpretation of these measurements is contentious, as they can also be replicated using other fractional states, such as $\nu = 7/3$. Our theory validates the Majorana picture using two key points: the inherent Ohmic dissipation present in resistive electrodes will distort the measured conductance curve, particularly making the majorana peak narrower compared to other peaks; and the magnitude of this distortion is directly related to the temperature and can be quantified using a dimensionless parameter. Utilizing this understanding, we propose a new method to differentiate the Majorana peak from competing fractional states based on their distinct conductance curve shapes. Our analysis suggests this technique could be applied to existing data, potentially confirming the Majorana energy spectrum.

Linear bandits, a type of contextual bandits, are commonly used to investigate a broad range of scenarios where arm characteristics might be missing or unreliable. Historically, bandit research has primarily focused on the setting where all arms have a defined context. In this study, we investigate a variant of linear bandits where each arm has a distinct context, yet some arms have no context at all. This scenario is known as linear bandits with diverse actions, and is notable for (i) being common in real-world situations where some actions simply mimic others and (ii) requiring a modified spectral analysis due to the presence of unobserved arms. We then use our newly derived analysis to demonstrate the first-order utility regret bounds for this unexplored scenario, applying a similar approach as in vanilla linear bandits. However, our work reveals that a widely-used inference method in linear bandit settings may result in inconsistent estimates, even in very large setups, even when all arms have a defined context. This highlights a previously unrecognized issue of inference instability in linear bandit settings. To address this issue, we propose an alternative inference method which yields more reliable results and is especially beneficial in linear bandit settings involving unique contexts.

Graphene with gaps has drawn attention, particularly due to its unique properties combining with the orbital Hall effect, which may lead to new insights into valley-Hall effects. By introducing an external magnetic field into this system, we identify a unique phenomenon where the orbital Hall effect replaces the valley effect, resulting in significantly greater conductivity. Our research uncovered that the cross-sectional current in the orbital Hall effect is significantly higher than that of the valley effect, with the former being infinite in certain configurations and the latter being directly proportional to the gate charge. This difference in cross-sectional current is the key factor explaining the significantly higher total current observed in the orbital Hall effect compared to the valley effect, especially when a significant magnetic field is applied.

In the realm of graph classification, reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective technique, particularly when dealing with imbalanced data distribution.  However, this issue is prevalent not only in imbalance between different class distributions but also when the output is contaminated with incorrect labels.  In this research, we investigate the impact of such label contamination in graph neural networks more closely, focusing on the aspects of node and graph node evaluation.  Our work not only maps the susceptibility of CNN and GNN models to this phenomenon but also develops a novel algorithm, RLCD, to address it.  Inspired by RL in balancing the risks and rewards, RLCD is designed to balance between accuracy and oversight, making the training process resilient to label manipulation.  Our study is conducted using two distinct graph neural networks, Graph Convolutional Networks and Graph Attention Networks, and evaluates the performance across different levels of label contamination.  Our analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of RLCD in outputing results unmarred by label contamination when compared to a baseline training method that relies solely on cross-validation, achieving a significant improvement of 10.21% in ABCD metric and 7.44% in AUC in GAT model and a 10.21% in ABCD metric and a 4.46% in AUC in GCN model.  Our research is made available through our public GitHub repository.

Virtual telescopes to offer photometry and homogenized photometric systems (HPS) are vital tools in scientific research, required for both extragalactic and galactic studies. These services are in high demand and must maintain extreme levels of quality and precision to be credible. To improve the accuracy and reliability of their data, operating microsecond levels on astrometry, a new approach has been presented to optimize the alignment of astronomical catalogs using astrometry and photometry. This method was validated through simulations and proved to reduce alignment offsets down to the precision limits of the individual catalog astrometry. When applied to real-world datasets, this approach has shown significant improvements with offsets decreasing from millions of tenth of an arcsecond to levels measured, with results including the alignment of two catalogs resulting in an offset of approximately thousandths of an arcsecond. Furthermore, this approach has enabled the identification of discrepancies between the two catalogs, with some objects showing differences of up to a second in right ascension and 2 minutes in declination, indicating possible artifacts or inaccuracies in the data provided.

For 3-uniform infinite hypergraphs, we establish a perfect matching in every minimal vertex subset when the subgraph formed by a specific number of p elements (with p greater than a certain value) has a connection density greater than the absolute value of a mathematical expression involving p and a constant variable. Furthermore, we present a counterexample where the subgraph's connection density is below this threshold, resulting in the absence of a perfect matching. Additionally, we prove that for specific types of 3-uniform hypergraphs, there exists a perfect matching in every vertex subset meeting a particular density criterion, with an associated lower bound on the number of vertices.

The success of ontology-based knowledge engineering in supporting the development of complex domain-specific ontologies has left scientists and engineers wondering how to effectively manage and visualize such large, intricate data sets. Although many visualization tools are available for exploring hierarchical data, there currently isn't a user-friendly, intuitive system accessible via the web that enables a thorough exploration of large non-hierarchical ontologies. In response to this need, a visualization system called OntoPlot has been designed to display and facilitate the exploration of large ontologies using an innovative, radial visualization. This system places the central concept at the center and hierarchical relationships on the periphery, while integrating interactive components to explore both types of relationships. OntoPlot allows users to view and explore large ontologies based on hierarchical or non-hierarchical relationships and to access related information via hyperlinks, all rendered in a user-friendly web interface. OntoPlot was used to create visualizations of two large ontologies: Guillardia and Chlamydomonas. These demonstrations not only showcase the efficacy of OntoPlot in exploring non-hierarchical relationships but also highlight its versatility in handling hierarchical relationships, thus making it a highly useful and versatile visualization and exploration tool.

This research explores a novel approach to automated speech transcription, utilizing a cycle-consistent training method to combine multiple domains and increase the method's effectiveness when limited training data is available. Three innovative techniques are developed: a cycle-consistent training method that enables the use of multiple domains, a method for identifying and disregarding inconsistent elements within training data, and an approach for improving performance on unseen domains by penalizing differences within a training dataset. Our findings demonstrate that this cycle-consistent training method produces high-quality transcripts across multiple domains, and that incorporating the two complementary techniques significantly enhances performance, particularly in unseen domains. Ultimately, our interdisciplinary model yields outstanding results, exceeding performance expectations in large and small datasets alike.

A fundamental issue in Artificial Intelligence that has received significant attention is the development of autonomous agents that can effectively navigate on their own. Despite the availability of suitable task descriptions, previous approaches failed to exceed moderately complex levels of difficulty within reasonable time frames. As such, they are not suitable for supporting more sophisticated autonomous systems like intelligent robots. In order to overcome these limitations, we are proposing a new method of logic-based reasoning called Profound Active Deduction (PAD). This novel approach enables a logic system to simultaneously consider an individual's knowledge, the available sensory inputs, and instructions from an external controller. Additionally, PAD allows for seamless interaction between different levels of abstraction, from high-level conceptual thinking to more specific, detailed processes. We have implemented an efficient version of PAD that operates in a forward-reasoning manner and tested it on a range of complex, geometric level control problems. Furthermore, we have successfully adapted the developed theory into a modular frame-work for autonomous systems called the PAD triple. In comparison to other existing systems, our approach has shown to be more efficient and capable of supporting more intricate navigation systems with shorter processing times.

The Soret effect, which describes the separation of components within a mixture under a temperature gradient, has been explored in a binary system composed of spherical molecules that interact via a soft repulsive force. The equilibrium dynamics of these molecules in thermal fluctuation have been used to simulate non-equilibrium conditions, resulting in the separation of components. The Soret coefficient, a measure of separation, has been calculated and analysed in relation to the molecules' size, relative interactions and the stiffness of their repulsive force. It was found that a soft repulsive force that begins at an infinitely soft interval but transitions to a finite deformation elasticity results in a Soret coefficient that can be both positive and negative, dependent on the relative interactions between components. This contrasts with previous research on systems composed of molecules with uniform stiffness properties, which only exhibited negative Soret coefficients. The variation in Soret coefficients due to varying stiffness was found to be significantly influenced by the size of the molecules in comparison to the pore size of the system. This effect was found to be particularly pronounced in systems composed of small molecules. The internal flexibility of molecules has been implicated as a key factor in determining the Soret coefficient, suggesting that flexible molecules separate more easily within a temperature gradient. This is particularly significant in systems composed of molecules that exhibit a high ratio of internal flexibility to size, such as those composed of proteins or biological membranes.

In the music domain, particularly with musical compositions and automatic generation, there has been growing interest in understanding what constitutes high-quality music. However, manual evaluation by experts is a time-consuming and inefficient process, hindering further research in this area. Conversely, non-experts may not accurately identify high-quality music, making their opinions less reliable. A novel paradigm for automated music composition evaluation has been developed, which utilizes a transformer-based language model to analyze criticisms provided by both expert and non-expert groups. By analyzing the criticisms, the model can validate whether a composition's perceived strengths and weaknesses are legitimate, leading to the establishment of reliable evaluation criteria. Compositional features, praised by non-experts and criticized by both experts and non-experts, were extracted through an analysis that conditioned on critic type. Conversely, features praised solely by experts were also identified, indicating the capability of the proposed system to detect complex, expert-driven appraisal criteria.

In pedestrian identification, a cascade classifier technique is widely utilized
to effectively reduce false positives and speed up identification processes up to
80 times. Nonetheless, cascade classifiers struggle when adapted to new domains
due to their lack of supervision, resulting in poor performance and high false
positives rates. To overcome this challenge, researchers often employ domain adaptation
methods for discriminative models. This study proposes a new approach, called the
box ordering method, which can be used to reorder features' difficulty levels in
pedestrian identification cascades without any need for supervision. This method
is then combined with offline domain adaptation, using a technique called distribution
alignment, to further optimize domain-adapted models. The experiment results
confirm the box ordering method's effectiveness in reducing false positives and
improving overall accuracy. Furthermore, a domain adaptation technique proved to
maintain the performance benefits of the box ordering method. Both the box ordering
and domain adaptation techniques are shown to work synergistically to yield better
outcomes.

This paper presents an innovative approach to enhance music created with neural composers, leveraging visual techniques and audio representation. Unlike conventional neural networks, which generate music through auditory signals, we explore the use of an alternative visual pathway. Furthermore, to expand the scope of music generation, we've developed a system that combines a conventional melodic representation with a neural composer trained on discrete spectrogram images. To facilitate communication between these systems, we've established two methods for converting images into melodies and adjusting existing melodies, all aimed at producing new music.

In this research, we record users throwing a virtual ball who are shown either a correct release point or an incorrect one, and we analyze the impact on their throwing movement. Our study reveals that an incorrect release point leads users to adjust their throwing motion in a specific way, which is particularly noticeable in the initial phase of the movement. Additionally, an investigation into user behavior with an incorrect release point suggests that the primary reason for errors in virtual throwing tasks is the underestimation of the required throwing distance. Lastly, our study demonstrates that an erroneous point of release in throwing motions can be realistically simulated by adjusting the initial position of the dominant hand.

Conventional machine translation models operate on a sequence-to-sequence basis, treating input and output in a linear fashion, despite comprising multiple layers of hierarchical structure. These models are inherently linear in both computation and storage, with no built-in awareness of their complex organization. As an attempt to address this limitation, a new type of decoding implementation is proposed, one that harnesses the hierarchical nature of neural machine translation. By leveraging tree traversal techniques, this decoding method, called top-down tree formed decoding, facilitates parallel exploration of different branches, thereby improving efficiency both computationally and in terms of storage. Additionally, a novel tree representation called the syntactic link tree is designed to capture the intricate relationships between words and maintain its structural integrity even across sentence boundaries, thereby allowing interpretation of neural machine translation. Experimental results on English-to-Greek translation datasets suggest that the proposed top-down tree formed decoding approach can enhance translation quality and reduce memory usage and decoding time compared to conventional methods, particularly for large and complex models. Notably, it was found that the syntactic link tree often exhibits a level of coherence that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods, including supervised and semi-supervised tree translation models.

Interstellar clouds transform over vast periods into more compact molecular cloud fragments through a long-term instability. This instability is caused by the consumption of excess gas atoms and molecules, whose binding energies range across several distinct categories. In order to grasp this universal phenomenon, researchers in the field of astrochemistry are adopting an approach from statistical mechanics, comparing experimental data on the gas's desorption energy to simulations based on the solid's energy level distributions. Despite this new understanding, there is still a significant gap in our knowledge regarding the energy level distributions of molecules on dust grains. In an effort to bridge this gap, we have developed the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, a comprehensive database of binding energy distributions for a wide range of molecules on graphite, silicate clays, and ice. This platform allows users to quickly access the energy distributions for a particular molecule or category of molecules, enabling a direct comparison to experimental data and future experimental results. The platform's comprehensive database includes over 400 distinct binding energy points for more than 150 distinct molecules and 13 distinct energy distributions. This platform is designed to support interdisciplinary collaborations between astronomers, astrochemists, and surface scientists to better understand gravitational collapse. In the future, we plan to expand the platform's content to encompass more complex ice layers and additional clustering reactions.

We analyzed the characteristics of a multiplicative stochastic model, determined its parameters by fitting data describing the COVID-19 pandemic in Mexico, and found that one fitted line adequately describes the initial increase in cases, revealing a common underlying pattern. Additionally, we discovered that both the initial increase in cases in Mexico and the overall pandemic trend worldwide can be explained using a constant multiplication factor and initial growth rate. This parameter set can also be used to describe individual country pandemic trajectories.

Quantum simulations of static many-electron systems' ground states employ unitary quantum circuits to represent the action of Hamiltonians. Despite the closest approximation with a quantum algorithm having an exponentially increasing depth, there has been little success in achieving an accurate classical approximation with circuits of a manageable depth. We present an approach called shallow shade, where a quantum circuit of a low depth is used to slightly modify a quantum state, after which a classical function is approximated through an average of measurements. This method achieves significant accuracy improvements in comparison to the previously most successful shallowest approach. Additionally, we apply this approach to various Hamiltonians, including a quantum version of the Ising model with a intermediate-scale chain, where the results are compared to high-depth and deep classical simulations. This method is reported to be available at deepfakes.org.

The researchers in this study examine the two-dimensional Davey-Stewartson II equations, a combination of shallow water equations and their corresponding nonlinear Schrödinger equation coupling. They are interested in understanding how solutions behave over long periods of time in a region with a varying coordinate system near a specific type of singular point. To address this, they first simplify the equations into a nonhomogeneous linear equation and then analyze the behavior of the associated scattering problem. Notably, the Riemann-Hilbert formalism and the long-wave asymptotic behavior reveal an important feature of the reflection coefficient, which decays at a certain rate proportional to $|k|^{-1/2}$. This study is significant in understanding the long-time behavior of the original problem.

To improve the reliability of text classification when working with incomplete or uncertain text data, we are developing advanced language generation models that can generate multiple alternative versions of text, each representing a plausible interpretation of the input. These "Sibylvariant" models are based on an idea from ancient mythology. In addition to generating new text, we are exploring methods for selectively accepting or rejecting the original text or one of the generated alternatives during the inference process. Through our studies on benchmark datasets, we have found that "Sibylvariant" classification models can outperform their standard counterparts by at least 0.8 points in terms of mean average precision, while also providing significant improvements in robustness and reliability when applied to real-world hate speech detection tasks. These models will be made publicly available as pre-trained, full end-to-end models, providing a useful resource for other researchers.

We explore the concept of meta-learning, where an AI algorithm adapts to new problem structures. Although meta-learning has gained significant interest in the past few years, it remains challenging due to two main issues: limited access to new tasks, and a lack of understanding on existing methods. To address this, we developed MesoNet, a robust learning approach for graph classification that relies on minimal task-specific training. By using graph representation learning, MesoNet proves effective on a range of graph classification problems. Furthermore, our research highlights the trade-offs between domain expertise and available data. MesoNet's performance is evaluated on 19 unique chemistry-related tasks, where it consistently outperforms baseline models by providing accurate and interpretable results. Additionally, our study examines the impact of our approach on relative chemical importance assessments, enabling the accurate identification of relevant properties.

Knowledge distillation is a well-known technique used to simplify large language models, with advantages in computational efficiency and data requirements. Our research explores the robustness of a simplified model, created using knowledge distillation with a multi-language transformer, to have its internal knowledge transferred to other tasks through classification quantization. We found that distillation produces better results in our model, specifically in its ability to handle new languages with reduced data requirements, whereas quantization produces more reliable and accurate results in its ability to handle existing languages. However, both techniques show similar levels of instability when applied to new languages with small data requirements, highlighting the importance of a solid initial foundation in successful knowledge distillation. Additionally, we found that the success of knowledge distillation is not solely dependent on the teacher model's accuracy, but rather its ability to accurately reproduce the student model's responses, which in turn is influenced by the data requirements.

Consider a hypergraph with a rooted node, denoted as $r$, and an even number of edges, $m \geq 2$, that connect the root to distinct sets of vertices. We define a hypergraph as r-uniform when all its edges contain the root node and have a constant number of vertices. A hypergraph is r-uniform and 2-colorable if its structure can be represented by two distinct color patterns using the root node as red $r_t$ and the remaining vertices as blue $b_v$. With some basic constraints, a Lagrangian function for a rooted and r-uniform hypergraph is defined as a mathematical expression that results in zero for red vertices and a positive value for blue vertices. Although our research does not yield a complete solution, a number of possible cases and minimal constraints for the values of hypergraph edges are identified. Specifically, if the edges include at least three blue vertices, then their sum can be bounded between $\frac{4m^2}{9}+O(m)$ and $\frac{4m^2}{9}+4m+3$, approximately. If the edges contain exactly two blue vertices, then their sum can be bounded between $2\frac{m}{3}+M(r,h)$ and $2\frac{m}{3}+\tfrac{4}{3}m+3$, where $M(r,h)$ represents the maximum possible value of a certain mathematical expression that is dependent on

In image segmentation, we often rely on substantial amounts of annotated data, which can be scarce and costly to obtain, particularly for medical applications. This study explores the potential to reduce labeled data requirements for a specific task, namely pneumothorago (Pneumo) segmentation, by leveraging image processing techniques to enhance the effectiveness of a trained neural network, even when using fewer labeled examples. To achieve this, we utilize a combination of non-linear image enhancement methods, which preserve the statistical characteristics of the input images and incorporate a supervision term to refine the network's output based on the available annotated data. By doing so, we can obtain improved segmentation results for a Pneumo segmentation task with a notably reduced need for labeled data, demonstrating the efficacy of this augmented learning approach.

Although image description generation has been studied for decades, it still lacks
a fundamental understanding of what aspects are being described. To address this,
we developed a novel method for deriving descriptions from a small set of
semantic templates. A large corpus of high-quality templates can be obtained
without manual labeling, and previous research has already explored methods for
obtaining such datasets. Our method enables image description generation with
meaningful components by using a pre-trained template encoder and refining the
coefficients through self-training. Experimentally, our method outperforms other
state-of-the-art methods in describing objects using local features without
having an object-level annotation. Moreover, our description-generated images
exhibit greater consistency with semantic templates, resulting in improved
description quality.

This research delves into a variety of damage concepts, illustrating both dependent and independent relationships between agents. Specifically, it defines and illustrates rearward damage caused by the actions of an agent in the past influencing another's current state. In such cases, causal diagnosis is enhanced by incorporating past causal effect constraints. In addition, scenarios involving concurrent effects from multiple damaging events are examined, incorporating both overlapping and non-overlapping causes. These are formulated as integrated causal models, parameterised in a probabilistic and adversarial frameworks. Solving these models yields optimal damage identification mechanisms, whose adversarial training data offer a natural measure of effectiveness. Finally, dependent damage is explored through a dynamic game model, where one agent's past actions are influenced by another's foresight of future consequences.

This study showcases the capabilities of MMLSpark, an open-source library that merges Python 3.x and Scala within a single environment. By combining Python 3.x for dynamic machine learning model development and Scala for real-time big data processing, MMLSpark offers a powerful partnership. We will focus on specific MMLSpark components including Python 3.x auto-scaling deep neural networks and Scala integration with Python. This paper will present two practical applications, such as using MMLSpark to detect chaos in time series data, including songs, and predicting user behavior from online event logs. Additionally, we will illustrate MMLSpark's potential through a visual analysis of neural networks, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-time feedback.

We're giving vision a break by leveraging pre-trained visual models without
requiring them to be fine-tuned on our specific task. This approach allows us
to utilize ensembles of multiple models, explore different vision models,
shed light on their underlying mechanics, and achieve better performance. In
this study, we apply this concept to speech, exploring zero-shot speech
translation, domain adaptation, and style transfer across various languages and
domains. Unlike visual tasks, zero-shot speech tasks have been scarce due to
the need for precise target-conditioned speech generation, which lacks reference
speech examples and corresponds with a specific speaker. To address this, we
develop a novel latent space visualization technique that enables disentangling
perceptual and prosodic features without prior knowledge of the specific
speakers, languages, and domains involved. Furthermore, we introduce a new
speech synthesis dataset for low-resource languages, which shows that our
approach successfully applies without requiring a training set. Experiments
are conducted using 10 different speech synthesis models, and results are
evaluated using both objective and subjective metrics.

This work introduces a novel extension of Coleman-Gurtin theory, exploring the properties of classical thermodynamics within a confined, internally stressed solid. The investigation focuses on the interplay between surface anomalies and the presence of external forces. It is discovered that active mutations, akin to those observed in bacteria, can be viewed as a specific form of surface anomaly. Our study is structured as follows: (i) We establish a general theoretical framework by incorporating surface-related inequalities and superpotential functions that adhere to thermodynamic consistency. (ii) We then derive governing equations, including a dynamic system characterized by non-linear, non-local, and non-inertial behavior. (iii) To illustrate the applicability of this theory, we examine the universal system - a stressed solid subjected to time-varying external forces and stress-dependent surface conditions. Furthermore, we delve into the historical context of active mutations, providing an overview of the existing literature and distinguishing them from other surface anomalies.

Final load, representing the low voltage grid's consumption, is typically forecasted in two stages: large and small area analysis. We examine improvements in forecast accuracy for large area finals, specifically those related to daily peak consumption. Three different models for final peak prediction are evaluated: ARIMA, the ETS rule, and the ARIMA-ETS combination. Historical usage data from Dreo and ESO in 2021 were used for analysis, and results indicate a significant increase in prediction accuracy (up to 30%) when the combination of the two methods is utilized.

Domain expertise integration is an intricate process of combining a domain expert's input with a machine learning model in a data analysis pipeline. Unfortunately, there is no unified guidance available for incorporating domain experts' knowledge into these models. To address this, we have created a comprehensive dataset consisting of 33 distinct tasks that encompass various forms of knowledge and sensitivities, and propose a five-step framework for embedding domain expertise into each task. This framework accounts for the expert's level of insight into each task, considers any associated risks, designs methods for integrating their knowledge, trains and evaluates the resulting integrated model. We have tested our framework with a dataset comprising 10 studies across three distinct fields, namely law, medicine, and physics. We have found that incorporating domain experts' knowledge through our proposed framework leads to improved performance, particularly in fields such as law where incorporating their knowledge results in significantly more accurate outcomes. Additionally, we have found that our framework allows for the quantification of the domain expert's level of insight and involvement on a numerical scale. Further experiments on a dataset containing 16 additional fields demonstrated that our framework's trained models are generally competitive with state-of-the-art results, and that further research is required to overcome existing challenges in these fields.

The current COVID-19 segmentation datasets are heavily skewed towards upper lung regions due to a higher prevalence of symptoms in the upper chest area. This partiality poses challenges for using existing segmentation methods that rely solely on annotations from the majority region. To address this imbalance, we propose the development of a new segmentation framework that incorporates weakly supervised learning. This approach can automatically generate a balanced distribution of annotation areas. To achieve this, we create a balance detection model that finds a supplementary region to compensate for the initial annotation. The supplementary region is then merged with the initial annotation to form a complete dataset for training the segmentation model. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework is effective in obtaining a balanced distribution of annotation areas from the publicly available SARS-CoV--2 Pneumonia dataset. Furthermore, the framework exhibits superior performance in comparison to traditional methods that rely solely on the initial annotation, with a balanced upper and lower region distribution. The framework's efficacy in tackling imbalanced COVID-19 lesion segmentation is also validated through a additional experiment conducted on the SARS-CoV-2 CT dataset. The framework achieved high accuracy with a Dice coefficient of 0.90, with notable balance in upper and lower lung region performance. With the advancement of the existing framework, it is now possible to perform upper and lower lung region comparison automatically. With the advent of the new framework, it is possible to the performance of the segmentation model evaluated using multi-region performance. The framework was released on: https://github.com/grad

Accurate vertebrae positioning is a crucial step in spinal image analysis. Although automated segmentation techniques exist, they frequently fail without expert intervention, resulting in vertebrae identification errors. Most prior studies directly aimed to identify vertebrae from image data, but this approach often leads to incorrect spine orientation and vertebrae correlation. Without correct orientation and correlation, it is challenging to design effective segmentation methods. In this paper, a groundbreaking approach is proposed to rectify the spine and enhance vertebrae characteristics through an anatomically constrained optimization process. Once the spine is aligned and the vertebrae are enhanced, they can be easily detected through thresholding and morphological operations. This method's effectiveness under different, prone, and supine positions is verified on a large dataset from 1,000 subjects, outperforming the state-of-the-art commercial IDNet method in vertebra detection and positioning. Furthermore, to make this method applicable in multi-center scenarios, a robust dataset-independent training strategy is developed to adapt the approach to different datasets without the need for prior training data. As a result, the proposed pipeline exhibits superior performance in vertebra identification and positioning, according to evaluations using multiple publicly available datasets.

Our research focuses on electron collisions with a proton surrounded by a strong quantized light field, occurring within the regime of extremely strong light-matter coupling. We demonstrate how frequent oscillations and boundary changes between the light field and proton lead to temporary shifts in energy, causing an unstable state. However, due to fluctuations in quantum measurements, a pathway to a more stable state emerges, caused by a shift in phase, through electron collisions that resonate at specific energy levels. This electron-proton interaction can potentially be observed using experiments involving laser and electron beam interactions.

In recent years, particularly in robotics, an increasing number of researchers have explored the capabilities of elastic actuators as a cost-effective alternative to traditional actuators. Despite their potential, these actuators require careful integration into existing robot systems, presenting a significant engineering challenge. To address this, we developed a novel approach where an elastic actuator can be incorporated into existing quadruped robots without the need for extensive redesign. This approach utilizes reinforcement learning and dynamic simulation to determine the optimal motor drive signals for given tasks, without modifying the robots' underlying architecture. We evaluated the efficacy of this method through extensive simulation tests, as well as by conducting experiments on an elastic actuator without any modifications to the underlying hardware. The results demonstrate that this approach can successfully replicate the movement of traditional actuators, while also allowing for variable impedance adjustment. This mobility paradigm enables researchers to reframe existing quadruped robots as general-purpose platforms for investigating elastic mobility, thereby unlocking new avenues for research and investigation.

We introduce a new variational method to examine quantum dynamical divisibility, which can be applied even in the presence of uncertainty. The proposed method acknowledges the initial state's influence on the divisibility criterion, and we demonstrate its applicability to several notable models, including Lorentz-Ising and Heisenberg models.

A laboratory study conducted in a small, specially controlled plasma device discovered a mini tear in a thin, flat plasma cloud, identical to a larger phenomenon that occurs in sun's atmosphere. Researchers tracked the tiny rift's progression and found that it was triggered by an irregularity in the plasma's density, which was then escalated by an irregular energy fluctuation. As it grew, the rift created and left behind smaller and larger-scale irregularities in its path, similar to a chain reaction of a chain snap. Studies of the rift's behavior provided valuable insights into how plasma behaves in the sun's atmosphere, particularly in relation to how different particles interact in this environment.

A novel fashion retrieval system has been developed that utilizes a unique feature-level trait manipulation approach has been devised. This method enables the modification of identifiable characteristics in images, such as sleeves or hats, without affecting the underlying content. The system leverages a semi-supervised framework to manage the time-consuming process of labeling individual body parts in images. By training a network with a shared encoder and distinct decoders for different traits, the feature-level manipulation has proven to be accurate and robust. The introduced paradigm is generalizable and can be applied to a wide range of image retrieval tasks beyond the fashion domain.

The non-linear inverse problems involving operators between infinite-dimensional spaces are a notable category of ill-posed problems characterized by a infinite-dimensional target function represented through its operator applied to an infinite-dimensional variable. A convergence theory is developed for a dual gradient approach that involves two infinite series, one non-decreasing and the other decreasing with potential functions related to an T-stable quasi-convex problem whose conjugate is quasi-concave in relation to the dual variable's pairing with the problem's constraint and the variable's pairing with the problem's constraint's dual. A general theorem is developed for the problem of minimizing a non-positive homogeneous convex function, with an alternative expressing the convergence speed of the algorithm through an lower bound on step size. By applying this model to a problem of reconstructing an function from its Fourier coefficients, a speed of convergence of $\ln(1/k)$ is obtained, with time of computation of $k$. Furthermore, the algorithm is implemented in the context of the Fourier transform, with an analysis of its efficiency in the context of the Fourier transform's finite sampling, with a computational time of $k$ as $O(N)$. Finally, the computational method is implemented using the GPU, with a computational method using the GPU that utilizes the Fourier transform's coherence in parallel processing.

An emerging area of research, light field computing, holds significant potential in creating immersive 3D environments and revolutionizing our understanding of the physical world. A crucial component of light field computing, light field depth estimation, is still an unresolved challenge, particularly when encountering occlusion issues. In response, we introduce the Occlusion-Responsive Expense creator (ORC), a flexible and adaptable model for light field depth and occlusion estimation. By leveraging patch-based encoding and dynamic cost assignment, ORC is capable of efficiently estimating depth and occlusion throughout various light field datasets. We demonstrate ORC's performance using sub-aperture array and four-dimensional light field data from established datasets, such as NLIFD-DB, as well as recent datasets EPICLightField and the AmericasCat Dataset. Furthermore, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

This study applies the bilinear method to derive a novel set of the Fokas-Lenells equations' square operator's inverse solution, thereby providing an alternative means of verification for recently discovered direct integration techniques within the Fokas-Lenells family. The derived solutions are expressed in terms of hyperbolic CS/DS functions, offering a comprehensive comparison with existing solutions from the Ma method, which is subsequently extended to obtain new hyperbolic CS/DS function based solutions for the Fokas-Lenells equations.

A theoretical framework is introduced to derive a class of non-unified gravitational theories with non-metricity, encompassing a subset of Poincaré-2-algebra-based models. These theories can be viewed as manifestations of higher-spin gauge fields within a non-dual, non-Lagrangian framework. Conversely, they can also be seen as being derived from a dual action principle. Utilizing a generalized De Donder construction and an extended Palatini variation method, we provide two distinct approaches to formulate the actions for non-metricity gravity, one of which is accompanied by a corresponding field theory can be found in the reference at the end of this document.

To meet the rapid growth in demand for network services, networks must often be expanded by installing additional access points. These access points can be deployed either intentionally to cover neglected areas or inadvertently due to inadequate installation, resulting in overlap between new and existing access points. To optimize the performance of these networks, it is essential to identify the cause and nature of interference and make informed decisions about incorporating additional access points and their specific location. This research aims to address this issue by developing an innovative AP choice rule based on the IEEE 802.11k/v standards, which enables accurate assessment of expected signal quality from a client device to any access point or extender within its network.

We began this study by collecting data on 11k/11v signals from a five-story building equipped with 11ac dual-band routers and measured the signal strength received by each device across all floors. To simulate various network configurations, we used the measured signal strength as a relative strength metric. Based on these measurements, we developed separate models to predict the expected signal strength from a client device to each access point and extender using a generalized model, which incorporates the effects of Hall-of-Fame, Hall-of-Failure, external interference, and fusion signals. This model's accuracy was verified by comparing its predictions to actual measurement data. Subsequently, we developed an algorithm grounded in the expected signal strength model to determine the optimal choice between a nearby access point and an extender for a client device to maintain a stronger network connection. To
